Early February, two in the morning, the flat in Cotroceni. Carmen went back to Madrid at the end of January; Mihai has one more week of leave. Rosa Elena is almost three weeks old and sleeps in her own room, under the hook where the ubugi used to hang.
(Whispering) Is she asleep?

Good. Then let’s go to sleep too. It’s already two o’clock.
(Yawning) That’s exactly what I was about to do. …Good night.

What could it be this time? She’s only just had her milk.

(A little later) Mihai, how is it going?

(Whispering) Careful. The door creaks.

to-ko-ro: three even syllables, a short “o” each time, and a lightly tapped “r” (like the “tt” in American “butter”, not rolled). In fast speech, “～て いる ところ” sounds like “～てる とこ”.
o-mu-tsu: “tsu” is one single sound, like the “ts” in “cats” followed by a barely whispered “u”. お-し-っ-こ: っ is a short pause, like a little catch of breath before “ko”.
nen-nen ko-ro-ri yo: ん lasts as long as a whole syllable (ne-n-ne-n = four beats). The lullaby is sung slowly and smoothly, with the voice falling at the end.
1. ところ: not just “place”, but also “the moment” of an action

You learned ところ meaning “place” (しずか な ところ, ch. 12). But ところ also means the “point” you’re at in an action — like a spot on a timeline. The verb form in front tells you exactly where you are: before, in the middle, or right after.
Verb form
Where you are on the timeline
dictionary form + ところ
BEFORE (about to start)
I’m just about to go to bed.
IN THE MIDDLE (happening right now)
RIGHT AFTER (has just finished)
She has just fallen asleep.

After ところ comes だ / です (or だった / でした). English often uses “just” for very different moments (“I’m just going to bed” vs “she’s just fallen asleep”), so pay attention to the verb form: ねる ところ (not asleep yet!) and ねた ところ (already asleep) are exact opposites.
Memory trick: picture a train. ～る ところ = the train is still at the platform and the doors are closing; ～て いる ところ = the train is moving; ～た ところ = the train has just arrived and the doors are opening.
2. ～る ところ: “about to…” and ～る ところ だった: “was just going to…, when…”
Dictionary form + ところ = the action is ready to start, this very instant. It’s often used with いま, ちょうど, これ から.
That’s exactly what I was about to do: go to bed.
I’m just about to leave.
Now I’m putting her in the cot (I’m about to).
In the past, ～る ところ だった (でした) says “I was just going to…”, and usually something happens that stops you. Very often it’s followed by のに or が: ねる ところ だった のに、なきだした.
A close variant: ～(よ)う と して いた ところ = “I was just getting ready to…” (the volitional from ch. 30 + と する = to try, to set about). Mihai: ちょうど いま、うたおう と して いた ところ だ よ.
Don’t mix up ～る ところ and ～る つもり (ch. 30). つもり = intention, maybe for tomorrow or next year. ところ = right now, in the next few seconds. ✗ らいねん にほん へ いく ところ です → ✓ らいねん にほん へ いく つもり です.
3. ～て いる ところ: “right now, in the middle of the action”

～て いる on its own describes an action in progress (ch. 10) or a state. ～て いる ところ zooms in on THIS very moment: “I’m right in the middle of it, don’t interrupt me”. That’s why it’s perfect on the phone and for apologies.
On the phone
Sorry, I’m eating right now.
Someone is rushing you
I’m doing it right now!
Answer to “what are you doing?”
The difference in nuance: いま おむつ を かえて いる = “I’m changing the nappy now” (a piece of information). いま おむつ を かえて いる ところ = “I’m right in the middle of changing it” (so I can’t do anything else, wait).
～て いる ところ only works with actions that unfold over time. With the state verbs from ch. 10 (けっこん して いる, すんで いる, しって いる) it isn’t used: ✗ マドリード に すんで いる ところ です.
4. ～た ところ: “have just finished”
Past form + ところ = the action has just ended, a few moments ago. It goes very well with いま, ちょうど, さっき (a moment ago).
She drank her milk and has just fallen asleep.
I’ve just finished my piano practice!
She’s only just had her milk (and she’s still crying).

～た ところ means “it ended RIGHT NOW”, so it does NOT work with きのう, せんしゅう or “a month ago”: ✗ きのう ねた ところ です. For “I’ve (recently) just…”, even when more time has passed, Japanese has ～た ばかり — we’ll learn it in the next chapter.
Notice のに from ch. 44: のんだ ところ な のに. ところ behaves like a noun, so before のに it takes な (like やすみ な のに).
5. ～ところ に / へ, ～ところ を and “almost”: ～ところ だった
Because ところ is a “moment”, it can take particles, like any noun:
just when (something unexpected comes along)
Just as I was changing her, she peed again.
just in time
You came back just in time.
the moment when (you see it, photograph it)
He was watching her give the baby milk.
almost (but it didn’t happen)
a close call (something bad nearly happened)
That was close!

Watch the difference: ねる ところ だった = “I was just going to sleep” (and I didn’t). もう すこし で おこす ところ だった = “I almost woke her up” (but luckily I didn’t). The context and もう すこし で show you that it’s about a danger avoided.

Culture: in Japan, many young mothers go back to their parents’ home for the birth and the first weeks (さとがえり しゅっさん). At about one month, the baby is taken for the first time to a Shinto shrine (おみやまいり), dressed in a festive garment. Ana doesn’t have her parents nearby, but she had Carmen until the end of January, and Elena comes every day.

はじまった ところ — It has only just begun
On 18 January, Rosa Elena came home for the first time.
When they got out of the taxi, Mrs Doina was waiting for them at the top of the stairs: “Welcome home, Rozița!”
And Mr Petre’s dog was happily wagging its tail too.
Mrs Doina peered at Rosa Elena’s face: “Oh my, the spitting image of Mihai!”
When they walked into the flat, it smelled wonderful: Kenji was just heating up the soup.
“You’re back just in time. I’m about to boil the noodles.”
Before that, Ana took down the ubugi hanging on the wall: the one Mrs Fumiko had sewn from her mother’s kimono.
When they put it on her for the first time, it was a little big, but the cherry-blossom pattern suited Rosa Elena very well.
That evening they all ate Ramen Hana-chan and celebrated her coming home from hospital. The soup in the freezer went down a little more.
The morning of 20 January was the day Kenji was going back to Madrid.
Just as he was putting on his shoes at the door, Rosa Elena woke up and whimpered softly.
Kenji took his shoes off and came back. “I was just about to leave, but just a little longer.”
Kenji gently squeezed her tiny hand: “Next time we meet, I’ll make a ramen just for you.”
When he turned around in the doorway, Kenji’s eyes were red. “Got some steam in my eyes.” Except there was no ramen in the hallway.
Even after the door had closed, Mihai stood in the hallway for a long time.
At the end of January, Carmen went back to Spain too.
Before leaving, Carmen taught Ana how to bathe a baby: “You support the neck like this… Yes, very good.”
“I’ve only just got used to it, and now you’re leaving…”, Ana said, and Carmen laughed and hugged her.
“You’re a mother now. You’ll be fine.”
From then on, Elena came every day at lunchtime with soup she had made herself. “While I hold her, you sleep,” she would say, and send Ana off to the bedroom.
February was a sleepy month. Rosa Elena woke up every two or three hours and cried.
They had decided to get up in turns. But in reality, they both always woke up.
Mihai, next to them, rubbed his sleepy eyes and watched Ana give her the milk.
While Mihai held her, Ana would fall asleep without realising it.
One night, Mihai, half asleep, almost put sugar in instead of formula. If Ana hadn’t noticed, it would have been sweet milk. “That was close…”
On 10 February, Mihai’s leave came to an end.
In the morning, just as Mihai was getting ready to leave, Rosa Elena burst into tears. Maybe she was saying: “Daddy, don’t go.”
At the hospital, in the middle of a meeting, he almost fell asleep.
Dr Ionescu laughed: “All new dads are the same. Back in my day, I actually did fall asleep.”
During his lunch break he got a photo from Ana: Rosa Elena asleep in Elena’s arms. “She’s just fallen asleep. Hang in there, Daddy.”
One Saturday in mid-February, Ioana came to visit with flowers and a little picture book.
“Shall we take a break from Japanese practice for a while?” Ioana asked, but Mihai shook his head: “No, I want Rosa Elena to hear it too.”
So they spoke Japanese in front of Rosa Elena. She stared at their faces. “Maybe she already understands Japanese,” Ioana laughed.
Before Ioana left, Mihai took a photo of her holding Rosa Elena.
One Sunday at the end of February, they had a video call with Hiroshima. In Bucharest it was nine in the morning, in Hiroshima four in the afternoon.
“I’ve just finished my piano practice!” said Sakura, pressing her face up to the screen. “Sing Hana-chan your lullaby!”
Then, seeing Hana-chan in the pink socks, she was delighted: “They’re not baggy any more!”
Mihai, a little embarrassed, started singing: “Hush-a-bye, I’ll get angry, I’ll get angry…”
Sakura doubled over laughing: “Big brother, that’s wrong! Not ‘I’ll get angry’, it’s ‘go to sleep, little one’! You’re not allowed to get angry!”
Because he had learned it by ear from the CD, Mihai had been singing it wrong the whole time.
Ana laughed until she cried too: “All this time you’ve been singing ‘I’ll get angry’…”
Haruka said, laughing as well: “But Hana-chan fell asleep nicely, didn’t she? Next time I’ll teach you the correct song, properly.”
On the morning of 1 March, the snow outside had started to melt.
Mihai brought two little boxes. Inside each was a small ornament with a white and red string: a mărțișor.
“In Romania, on 1 March you give this to the people you love. It’s a sign that spring has come.”
He pinned one on Ana’s chest, and tied the other to Rosa Elena’s cot.
Ana gently touched the mărțișor on her chest and smiled: “What a lovely sign.”
At lunchtime Grandpa called from the village: “I’m drying the cherry wood for the little stool right now. It’ll be ready by summer.”
That evening, when Mihai came home from the hospital, Ana came running to the door.
“She’s just smiled! For the first time she really smiled!”
Mihai even forgot to take off his coat and went to the cot. But Rosa Elena had already gone back to her serious face.
“I missed the very best part.”
Mihai sat down next to the cot and sang softly. This time he at least got “go to sleep, little one” right.
Then Rosa Elena gazed at Mihai’s face, opened her little mouth slightly and gave a big smile.
“She smiled…” Mihai’s voice trembled. Ana caught that moment on her phone.
That night, at two o’clock, the crying was heard again. Mihai sat up in bed and smiled.
“Right, I’m on my way.”
Outside, the snow was melting and you could hear the quiet sound of running water.
Ana looked at Mihai with sleepy eyes and said: “Our job as parents has only just begun.”

Mime 6 actions (eating, getting dressed, writing, drinking tea, putting on shoes, opening the door). For each one say three sentences out loud: ～る ところ, ～て いる ところ, ～た ところ.
Act out a phone call: someone calls you at bad moments. Answer every time with ごめん、いま ～て いる ところ なの… and offer to call back later.
Tell out loud, in 1–2 minutes, a story about something that “almost” happened (もう すこし で ～ところ だった).
